Class 3 · Chapter 8 of 10

Picture charts, bars and tables

Read picture charts and bar charts, compare results and update a table.

  1. See it
  2. Try it
  3. Practise it
  4. Print it
  5. Check it

This chapter works best after Shopping totals and better buys. You can still look around, or jump to the check.

By the end I can…

  • I can use a picture-chart key.
  • I can compare values on a bar chart.
  • I can update a table or chart.

1 See it

Screen 1 of 4

Read the key

A picture chart has a key. Read it before you count.

Here each picture means 1 child, so 6 pictures means 6 children.

Screen 2 of 4

Read the scale

On a bar chart, look at the numbers up the side.

The cricket bar reaches 8. Football reaches 6.

Screen 3 of 4

Add bars together

How many children chose football or cricket? Add the two bars.

6 + 8 = 14 children.

Screen 4 of 4

Update the chart

2 children move from Cricket to Football. One bar goes down 2 and the other goes up 2.

Cricket becomes 6. Football becomes 8. The total stays the same.

Words to know
key
Tells you how many each picture or symbol stands for.
scale
The numbers up the side of a bar chart.
data
Facts and numbers you collect to answer a question.

For parents

What your child learns

Bar charts use a scale. Each gridline may stand for more than 1. Read where the bar ends and use the scale. To compare, subtract the two values.

A common slip

Children often read the grid squares as ones. Check what one square or line stands for before reading. Then multiply.

5-minute home activity: Draw a scaled chart

  1. Count 3 kinds of items at home, such as spoons, cups and plates.
  2. Draw bars on grid paper with 2 items per square.
  3. Read each bar using the scale.
  4. Find how many more one kind has than another.
